ECHOGEAR Swivel TV Stand - Universal Replacement Stand for TVs Up to 60"- Height Adjustable Up to 4" & Smooth TV Swivel - Works with Samsung, LG, Sony & More I got a new 50 inch 7 series samsung tv that has a curved back, so the screws that came with the stand does not fit. The required screws were M8 x 45mm, but the longest screws were m8 x 35mm. I'm ok with that as this screen is newer and has a different curve on teh back than most flatscreen tvs out there.

After a run to Fastenal to obtain the right length screws, everything installed fine. In order to level horizontal axis properly, I left the screws on the horizontal bar slightly loose. After putting on the screen, adjust for horizontal level, and then tighten the screws on the horizontal bar.

Only issue that i came into after that was the whole tv would lean backwards ever so slightly, like 4-5 degrees. Very noticeable since my tv is next to a door and bookcase. I noticed the problem was in the design of the vertical bars that are installed onto the tv itself.

The upper hook part that clips onto the top part of the horizontal bar is not the same thickness as the bottom hook part that sits on the lower part of the horizontal bar. Thin vertical top, thicker vertical bottom, you get a screen that is angled looking slightly up. Maybe its a design flaw or maybe its designed to accommodate heavier TV's that may cause the screen to lean forward (my tv was kinda light).

A fix for my TV leaning back was shoving a few shims under the back of the base plate to get it to lean more forward (i used a stack of like 8 business cards on both rear corners of the base plate; seems to work fine).

Overall, i'm happy with my product. The ability to swivel was the sole reason i bought this.
text_fidelity_b: ECHOGEAR Swivel TV Stand - Universal Replacement Stand for TVs Up to 60"- Height Adjustable Up to 4" & Smooth TV Swivel - Works with Samsung, LG, Sony & More

Osprey Apogee Men's Laptop Backpack , Kraken Blue This is a nice backpack. It’s lightweight and the color is very cool. It’s like a blue grey with dark teal straps. It’s not flashy but it’s not boring black either.
The 2 bottle holders on the side are very sleek and well done. It’s always annoying when bottles fall out is the side because they are too small - that won’t happen with these.
There are 3 pockets. The stash pocket is the only pocket that can be accessed if the compression hooks are used. The compression hooks can be tucked away when they aren’t needed which is nice - I don’t like having a bunch of hooks out catching on things.
The stash pocket isn’t huge but it’s a good size - can fit hand in easily and then it’s about 11” across.
The 2nd area is deep but isn’t wide. It will hold a jacket or sweater and then has 3 slotted pockets for a phone/ passport/ notebook. Outer 2 pockets are 3.5” and middle pocket is 4” wide. All pockets are about 5.5” deep.
The middle compartment also has a red clip. It’s easy to use and I like to use these to attach my keys so they don’t drop to the bottom of bags.
The main compartment is pretty big.
It has a double sided padded laptop area that measures 10.5” wide.
On top of the laptop is a tablet area that is single sided padded that measures 10” wide and up to 13” tall. The tablet area isn’t as deep as the laptop area. This area would also work for documents.
The top handle is well padded and sewn. Below that there is a two sided opening for headphone cords or even a plug to charge your laptop/tablet.
The main straps are well padded and adjustable. They have a top strap and a lower strap for comfort and security.
The zippers are all well quality and have a material flap over the top so it should keep anything inside pretty dry.
text_fidelity_b: Osprey Apogee Men's Laptop Backpack , Kraken Blue

I am also am finding it does a great job on a lot of other kinds of shots. I find I enjoy photographing birds--a tough subject--and have gotten some nice shots of them with this camera. The controls are easy to operate, conveniently located, and pretty easy to figure out even without resorting to the manual. I'm still doing a lot of experimenting with different settings to "learn" the camera's capabilities and get a feel for its sensitivity to light and its optics...an exercise highly recommended for folks like me who are new to cameras with manual controls. Have taken a few video clips with it that came out great.

The memory card it came with is kind of a joke--I bought a Kingston 2 GB card to use instead and have been real happy with that. It writes super-fast and I come nowhere close to ever running out of room (but I delete a lot of shots, too). Also, rechargeable batteries are HIGHLY recommended. I have three sets...one set lasted for three weeks of casual use--even with the LCD often open.

I've added a 52mm adapter tube and a few filters, plus a hood. Mainly I wanted the adapter and a UV filter to protect the lens for tight super-macro shots. One of these days I might get a wide angle lens. If you're going to be doing macro stuff or using the zoom a lot, use of a tripod will be key in getting clearly focused shots.

The sound quality is good, I’ve been using them with music and streaming shows, and I haven’t been disappointed with the sound quality.

I’m not as pleased with the short battery life, touch controls, and lack of audio cues.

I get about 2-3 hours of playback per charge. It’s rare for me to battery drain earbuds, but with this pair, I hear the low battery chime every time I use them.

The touch controls and lack of audio cues go together. The touch controls are super easy to activate on accident. More than once I’ve taken the earbuds out only to find I hit Play while doing so, and they kept playing music. Seagate 600 SSD 480 GB SATA 6 Gb/s 2.5-Inch 7mm Z-Height Solid State Drive ST480HM000 Though I have a laptop, I decided to use this solid-state drive as a boot drive on my desktop computer. If you are unfamiliar with the difference between a solid-state and a regular hard drive, the solid-state has no moving parts, which makes it silent, fast, reliable, and shock resistant. It has twice the capacity and twice the speed of the solid-state drive I got a couple of years ago for the same price, and blows away a standard drive for speed.

Given the silence and speed, it makes a great boot drive for running Windows, Photoshop, and other programs where speed is a huge advantage. Just to give you an idea, when upgrading from a regular two-year-old hard drive to this solid-state drive, my Windows boot time went from two minutes to about 10 seconds. Seriously, my computer now starts up and is ready to use in like 10 seconds.

What I do is use a solid-state drive as my boot drive and a regular hard drive as a storage drive. Solid-state drives like this are really expensive to purchase if you need any kind of capacity, but a 200 GB drive will certainly hold all of your programs and often used files.

As for this drive specifically, I hooked it up to my desktop and it was immediately recognized by Windows. The drivers installed automatically. In order to make the drive show up as a drive and work in Windows 7, I had to right-click on computer, click manage, double-click storage, double-click disk management, partition it, give it a drive letter, and format it.

As I said, it's a lot faster than the solid-state drive I had from a couple years ago, and there's no problem using it on my desktop machine rather than my laptop.
text_fidelity_b: Seagate 600 SSD 480 GB SATA 6 Gb/s 2.5-Inch 7mm Z-Height Solid State Drive ST480HM000

With vehicles, I am constantly getting notifications even though I have the camera set to exclude movement coming from the street. That function is definitely not working as it captures every car travelling down the block. The quality of the video is good during daylight hours or when an area is lit during darkness. text_fidelity_a:
Bestlight 48 LED Macro Ring Light With 6 Adaptors Rings for Canon Digital EOS Rebel SL1 (100D),T5i(700D),T4i(650D),T3(1100D),T3i(600D),60D,60Da,50D,Nikon D5300,D5000,D3000,D3200,D5100 DSLR Cameras I've always wanted a Canon macro flash but the cost was just too much for something that I would not use very regularly. This macro light, while not a flash, is a very affordable alternative that works very well.

It is a 48 LED light. There's no communication with the camera - it's not a flash, nor can it be controlled in any way by the camera itself. The controls are manual, and allow you to use all the LEDs, half of them (left) or half of them (right). It is powered by 2 AA batteries or by an AC adapter (included). The battery pack mounts on the hotshoe, and the macro light is affixed to the lens barrel.

The battery pack fit fine on my Canon 5D Mark II, but the manufacturer includes a note with the device that says an additional adapter will be needed for it to fit the hotshoe of Sony, Konica and Minolta DSLR cameras.

It comes with two diffusers (white and orange) that are easy to put on and take off. It also comes with six lens thread adapter rings for all the usual sizes - 49mm, 52, 55, 58, 62, and 67. You attach the adapter ring to front of lens, and slot the light over the ring.

No problems fitting it to a Canon L 100mm macro lens. Fit well and was secure during use.

It throws a good amount of light on a ultra close-range subject, which may be otherwise shaded by the close proximity of your lens, or for other reasons be hard to light properly. But, there are limitations - don't expect this to throw a lot of light like a light panel would on a subject at medium distance.

The build quality is better than expected given the price. It's all plastic, but seems more than durable enough for home use.

I'm very pleased with this. It's a small fraction of the cost of a Canon ring light and, while it does not have flash capabilities, it remains a very helpful addition to lighting those tricky macro shots. Highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Bestlight 48 LED Macro Ring Light With 6 Adaptors Rings for Canon Digital EOS Rebel SL1 (100D),T5i(700D),T4i(650D),T3(1100D),T3i(600D),60D,60Da,50D,Nikon D5300,D5000,D3000,D3200,D5100 DSLR Cameras

text_fidelity_a:
Contour +2 - Old Packaging (Discontinued by Manufacturer) This is a really cool camera in a lot of ways, and yet there are two things about it that I hate:

1) It writes *.mov files. Why would any company choose that over so many great standards out there? Quicktime is the norm for *.mov files, with other players claiming to play them, but often with issues. Quicktime is one of those programs that - even after you uninstall it and delete everything you can find associated with it in your registry - will hound you until the end of your days to upgrade and constantly ask permission to take over your computer, will change other file extensions to play on it without asking, etc. Therefore, I so loathe Quicktime that I generally won't even touch an *.mov file.

I'd even be tempted to take the product down to three stars because of this, but there is some chance that this was the only format that would allow them to include the GPS data. I sort of doubt it because Apple (Quicktime) is the most ridiculously proprietary company I can think of, but I guess I need to give Contour the benefit of the doubt. Same benefit of the doubt used for annoyance #2:

2) You need to install more software to see the GPS data. I hate installing more and more software on my computer because everything installed is just another chance to have something running as a service or process all the time, wasting your resources. In general, all software is more "bloated" than ever these days, making our more powerful than before computers unable to perform better than before.

I also wish for some Blackberry support, but they might have some with BB OS 10, supposedly. Frankly, I'm not that interested in the smart phone features; they just slow you down.

As I said, the camera is really cool, though, for its ease of use and its mounts. It's obviously geared toward adventurers and people that want to roll off roofs in shopping carts like that one show that used to be popular. It has a great feel to it in its construction and durability, but I want to make clear the very big caveat that these are the only reasons you want this camera. Besides the annoyances mentioned above, I have a couple point and shoot cameras that do 1080p video just as well (actually better, given their native formats) and they are smaller and cost less. But it is pretty awesome to mount this on your bike for those "just in case" scenarios.
text_fidelity_b: Contour +2 - Old Packaging (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

text_fidelity_a:
TRAM 7732 Satellite Radio Low-Profile Mirror-Mount Antenna [[VIDEOID:cbe7b798430f2aea6c124b1ed1015e2]] My husband has wanted a new antenna for his truck for quite some time. We had one with a long antenna in our wishlist for a year or more. We have, I would say, a middle class income, and only my husband works. We keep a pretty tight budget and sometimes needs and wants get weighed heavily.

The antenna he had finally started to really not work well and as I was going to purchase it (it would have been $22) he asked me to look for the low profile version. The low profile version, THIS version, ended up being $35, so more money. Presently, this antenna has been worth the money and made my husband VERY happy. He runs local and is home every night, but still, 16 hours a day in a truck, I want him to be happy. His Sirius radio makes him happy.

He installed this in about 15 minutes and the cabling goes in through a small waterproof port above his window that was already there. He drives a pneumatic bulk tanker daycab. The connection to his mirror is very secure. It is not a big ole antenna that says HERE I AM. It is very subdued.

Did he notice a difference? Yes! Not only does the sound now not break up because the wire on the old one was bad ... but THIS one seems to be more clear and does not lose signal at all. He pretty much just has an uninterrupted stream of music and news and whatever.

Very happy with our purchase and no complaints at all.
text_fidelity_b: TRAM 7732 Satellite Radio Low-Profile Mirror-Mount Antenna

text_fidelity_a:
Zip Ties 8 inch (1000 Pack), 40lbs Tensile Strength, Black Cable Ties, Wire Ties for indoor and outdoor use, by Skalon When it comes to zip ties; they either do what they're supposed to, or they don't. If you are simply expecting these to hold things together reasonably well, then they are perfectly adequate for the task. However, when I tested them by tying them to weights and using them to lift, I found that they broke about 1/2 the time at 30 pounds, never quite reaching 40 pounds.

They are reliably good for 20 pounds without breaking, which is not too bad, really, for something so small. While I feel that the 40 pound claim is somewhat misleading, they are actually comparable to most similar sized ties on the market as far as I can tell, and it's doubtful that most others would perform any better. If you're not using them to lift heavy weights then they'll work just fine, and you'd be hard pressed to find a better price for this quantity of similar ties.
text_fidelity_b: Zip Ties 8 inch (1000 Pack), 40lbs Tensile Strength, Black Cable Ties, Wire Ties for indoor and outdoor use, by Skalon

*Fast boot up times
*1080p screen

*Great feeling keyboard

Cons:
*None(Will update if I run into any)

text_fidelity_a: Mini DVD Player ARAFUNA, HDMI Small DVD Player for TV with All Region Free, Compact Small DVD CD/Disc Players with AV Output USB Input Remote Control and AV Cable I chose this DVD player for specific reason. My kids are not easy on DVDs, so scratches are galore. One even has a deep one that does not allow it to play anymore. This DVD player promised to play DVD/Blu-ray no matter what. And it truly does. It played our favorite cartoon Black Cauldron that has a deep scratch in the middle no problem. It plays Blu-rays well and the picture is brighter than on our old player. When paused the DVD player does not stay on for long and turns off rather quickly, but if you turn it on without switching DVD it starts playing from the same spot even if it's not Blu-ray DVD. The display is a bit simplistic and it took me a bit to figure out where to go to find flash card (Media Center button above the OK button will get you there). Fujifilm FinePix J40 12.2 MP Digital Camera with 3x Optical Zoom and 3-Inch LCD (Includes 2 GB SD Memory Card) The camera is $[..]for gosh sakes! It's an amazing little piece of technology. The 3X optics and 12.2MP CMOS camera are well matched in the optical train to provide a great image for casual photos adequate for most users. It's the simplest start-up I've ever seen. The viewer LCD provides a maximum size to the package. `The manual' is 7 steps of which 4 include inserting memory, battery, charging battery and turning it on. It's `point and shoot' in the extreme.

I work in the domain of optics & imaging design. My wife has a 5 year old Fuji camera of this same genre that I've gone to some lengths to compare with Nikon and Canon in this low cost market. Without getting technical ... for the old Fuji, there are no user discernable image quality differences. The Fuji optics were superior (i.e. best objective lens light capture and transfer). Take your pick between the 3 on the backend image processing system/PC interface.

My wife has carried the 5 year old Fuji in her purse every day ... that's a technically demanding reliability challenge. Fuji can be relied on to deliver the best value for money in an image capture platform if you're designing a million dollar platform or this $69 platform. You're not paying the premium for the huge advertisement budget of Nikon and Canon when you buy Fuji. I think you just get a better camera.

I can't speak to this unit's reliability for now. A 3x optical train with autofocus, f-stop, etc mechanisms and micro motors are robust to a point. They will all fail, even the highest dollar product, if exposed to the wrong environment (g-shock, sand, salt spray, thermal shock, etc).

One reviewer mentioned software loading problems. I had absolutely no problems on a Windows 7, 64bit OS.

You can't go wrong with this device. It's an excellent camera for you or the kids or the g-kids for Xmas.
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm FinePix J40 12.2 MP Digital Camera with 3x Optical Zoom and 3-Inch LCD (Includes 2 GB SD Memory Card)

I do not use this for work or gaming, I have a desktop for that. I was using a tablet, but honestly I hate it. I just can't adjust to typing on a touch screen, I want a real keyboard. I also hate fingerprints on my screen. I deal with it on my phone, but for a larger screen it makes me crazy. So I figured this would be a good solution, when it popped up for review. It fits comfortably on my lap and the screen is small enough I can see over it to watch tv, but large enough it is easy on my eyes. So far its been great, although I miss the left and right mouse buttons built into the touch pad area of most laptops. Maybe its a Chromebook thing, but I will just have to adjust.

I will say though it does feel a bit flimsy. I like the lightness, but in my lap typing I can feel the plastic body flexing. For the price I'd expect something a bit more durable, at least for the bottom half with the keyboard. The keys are responsive, although I'm use to my mechanical keyboard so switching to the thin chiclet style makes them feel mushier than they probably are. For a small laptop, they don't feel cramped and they are raised enough that I'm not miss-typing.

It was incredibly easy to set up, just entered my google log-in info and poof I was up and running. This would be a 5 star product if they hadn't just made it a bit sturdier.

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Keyboard 3G, Free 3G + Wi-Fi, 6" E Ink Display - includes Special Offers & Sponsored Screensavers This is by far the best ereader on the market.

The bad.

It doesn't do epub and it doesn't connect to the library. This seems like a deal breaker until you try to borrow a book from the library. I have one on hold now (to read on either the nook or the Sony) that should be available in 39 weeks. I'll probably give up and just buy it anyway.

The good.

The speed. The page turns are as fast as the average person can turn a print page. You won't see that "opening book" message the nook displays. When you tell it to open a book, it opens in less than a second. I keep hitting the page turn key just to marvel at how fast it is. I've never seen an ereader this fast. This is perfect.

Store access. Let me run you through buying a book for the various devices. For the Kindle, if you're on the Amazon site you select your book, click buy now, pick up the device and start reading. For the nook, you buy the book, then you turn on the touch screen that keeps turning itself off, you go into the home screen, go to "My Library", select "Update B&N Content" and wait a few minutes. There is no mechanism to automatically push content to the device. For the Sony (I'm using the Daily Edition, which has 3G), you use the custom software (no way to buy from a website), buy the book, then either transfer it via USB, or go to the device, to the store, log into your account (you need to provide your login information each time you go to the store) find the book you bought and click download, then wait. For buying from the device, Kindle is easy and fast, nook is decent, and Sony is unreasonably slow.

The screen. There is no glare, even with the book light on. It's the crispest and easiest to read screen out there. It's beautiful.

Audible integration. Download your books via WiFi or transfer via USB and listen with your device, either through headphones or the speakers. How cool is that? Now if only there were a card reader to store those larger files.

Collections. I have the Kindle 1, so I was first introduced to collections via Sony. It's great to be able to organize so much content. Here you can organize ebooks and audiobooks into collections together. That's one thing Kindle and Sony both have over nook--they treat content the same. Nook is the only one that doesn't let you annotate or bookmark newspapers and magazines, and who wouldn't want to mark an article to refer back to later?

Ease of use. I handed my Kindle 1 to a woman who was too scared of technology to turn on her own laptop. Her husband had to do it for her. I wanted to show her a passage in the Declaration of Independence, and I had the passage on the screen. I didn't instruct her. Moments later, she turned the page and just kept reading, all the way the end. Then she looked at what else I had on the device. An ereader should be as easy and intuitive to use as a print book, and most of us figured those out when we were about 10 months old. Kindle fits that bill.

Social networking. Post passages and comments on them to Twitter and Facebook. You can see what passages other readers have highlighted. This is particularly great for online book clubs.

More language sets. I'm kind of hoping Amazon will sell Japanese language books in the US Kindle store, or let us buy from Amazon.co.jp.

I could go on and on, but what it comes down to is, when it comes down to the core features of an ereader--buying, reading, annotating, and searching a book, Kindle beats the competition hands down. When it comes to extra bells and whistles--organization, commenting to others, web access, text to speech, Kindle beats the competition hands down.

There is no other viable choice any more. Kindle is just too much better than every other device out there.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Keyboard 3G, Free 3G + Wi-Fi, 6" E Ink Display - includes Special Offers & Sponsored Screensavers

text_fidelity_a:
Runner 60 Wireless Running Earbuds, Over Ear Hooks, 80-Hour Long Battery Life, Water-Resistant Wireless Running Headphones. Bass Boost, Bluetooth 5 Wireless Charging Case, Gift for Runners I switched from button-style earbuds, to this style-with ear loops to secure them to the outer ears due to constantly losing my regular earbuds when I worked out, or worked in the garden.

The sound quality on these is quite good for the price point, they stay in my ears very well, and I only lose one if I fall asleep with one in (that’s on me).

The only issue I have with these and Holy High’s over- the- ear buds, is that they can hit the high part of the inner part of my outer ear (pinna/auricle) where there is a cartilage high spot, which can be irritating if wearing for an extended time.
This is an issue with most over-the-ear buds, but it’s usually minimal if I’m not wearing them for long hours on end. These have become my favorite earbuds, if that tells you anything.

1 year update: I now own two sets of these (one purchased a year ago, and one purchased in the last 6-9 months I think), one in each color. Other than the price being about $10 higher than I think it should be, these are still working well for me. The sound is good for the price point, I don’t mind the soft touch button anymore, and I like these far better than my Comiso and HolyHigh sets. I always have an earbud in my ear playing audiobooks, music, streaming shows or taking calls, and these are still working. Will update if that changes.

I will say the Comiso brand has stopped even taking a charge months ago, and they’re about the same age as my black set of these Back Bay earbuds…
text_fidelity_b: Runner 60 Wireless Running Earbuds, Over Ear Hooks, 80-Hour Long Battery Life, Water-Resistant Wireless Running Headphones. Bass Boost, Bluetooth 5 Wireless Charging Case, Gift for Runners

I’ve had the dock on my desk for about three weeks now and like it a lot. My desk looks neater, the dock gives me all the ports I need on a daily basis without having to use multiple adapters, and it charges my laptop.

I didn’t need to download any extra drivers or software, the dock was plug and play for me. I’m using it with my Intel MacBook Pro (13-inch, 2017, Thunderbolt 3 ports). I had the ports replaced once but they are loose again, so a dock is extra useful for me -- I’m only plugging in one device instead of 3 or 4. And I don’t have to look for adapters for everything I want to plug in.

I have one external monitor plugged into the dock, using the HDMI port. I also tried connecting via DisplayPort and that worked just fine. I also have various USB peripherals plugged in. I like the arrangement of ports, most are in the back, but the dock has a USB 3.0 port as well as Micro SD and SD ports on the front, where you can easily swap flash drives and cards.

The only USB-C port is for connecting the dock to your computer. I would’ve liked a USB-C port to accommodate newer flash drives and phones, but that’s just because of my port problem on my laptop.

For my usage, mostly writing and streaming shows, the dock does not run hot.

text_fidelity_a:
Sony STRDH190 2-ch Home Stereo Receiver with Phono Inputs & Bluetooth Black While I might give this product four stars for being so basic and catering to the "just playing music off my phone" crowd, you can't argue with a product done right. And actually, for those who just play music off their phones, this is a huge step up from some Bluetooth speaker that so many people seem to have resorted to.

Basically, if you want a decent stereo for a room with no TV and you don't want to stream over the network (yes, you can do it through your phone, but that seems onerous at best), this is likely the stereo for you.

I like the Sony heft and quality, as well as classic design. I like that it has quite a few inputs including one with ground, and that it has an aux-in port in the front.

I love that you can do two sets of speakers, if you want to fill a large room evenly or if you want to cover two areas independently. You can also change from speaker A to speaker B to A+B to off via the remote, which my higher end 7.1 Sony stereo's remote cannot do (and that is annoying).

This is about perfect for my workshop (no TV, Internet streaming device nearby to give a physical output).

Speaker terminals are the cheaper-than-usual-for-Sony spring loaded type instead of 5-way posts. This is the least-premium feature of this stereo. No AM radio if you care.

I would sort of like an Ethernet interface, but properly accessing it without an external screen (which would require a video output that this receiver doesn't have) would be limiting.

Personally, I hate Bluetooth in this application, especially via phone, because you move to another room, the connection dies. I know a lot of people get through their lives with just the music on their phones, but there's always a better way. If you have one of those setups where you have a music player hooked to this and you can control that with your phone, that would be a pretty good setup.

Beautiful and robust receiver at a low price point if you don't aspire for other options. Great for a workshop or other TV-less space.
text_fidelity_b: Sony STRDH190 2-ch Home Stereo Receiver with Phono Inputs & Bluetooth Black

text_fidelity_a:
64G Mp3 Player with Bluetooth, Mp4/Story Player, Music Player, Supports FM Radio of High Volume Built-in Speaker, 4-Inch LCD Full Touch Screen, E-Book, Micro SD Card Slot Ups to 512GB (Black) It does what it's sold to do very well. I've tested several types of ebooks (PDFs, epub, doc, txt), mp3 files of various quality, pics, and vids (avi, x264, and x265) - it read and ran everything well and smoothly.
Basically it's a low-end phone running an old distro of Android. It's super locked down and there's no internet access, so there's no updating and no adding of apps - this includes bluetooth tethering. That being said, a few of the apps are ones I've used for ages and (obv) I like them: specifically moon reader, the ebook reader - it really works well on this device. And I believe the video player is MX Player, also an old fav. Moving files via TF card was a bit of a pain, as the older version of android only supports up to 4GB at a time, but otherwise it moved everything without error. I tested the reader with several cards, from a generic 32gb to a samsung 512gb u3, and they all read well, so you can easily have a large library of media at hand. There's no cam or wifi; and there aren't any sensors, so it can't tell tilt, ambient light, etc. The screen is tiny but looks surprisingly good. The speaker is decently loud, but it def sounds like a phone speaker, still though, it's better than expected.
If you just want a simple media device with some neat features (FM works really well btw), this is great. I both would and wouldn't recommend this for kids - you can't add any educational apps (or games, lol), and they wouldn't be able to access things like their school portal or wiki; but if you only want your kid to have books, vids, and audio with a few tools (calc, calendar, alarm), this is right up your ally. Heads up though, they can swap out the TF card if they have a media collection you don't know about, and Moon Reader supports requiring passwords for opening the app.
If you want something you can do more with, I'd suggest foregoing the 50% off coupon and getting a burner phone at this device's list price. A burner probably won't work as smoothly (because it will have more hardware/software), but it'll have wifi and an app store and updates.
I plan to use this as an extra/backup media device. I'm one of those weird people that has a TF collection in my bag with tons of movies, tv, games, etc. I'm going to put one of those pockets on the back for credit cards, and use a TF card organizing card to hold my cards, so I'll have all my media together and with a device that can play them, in case my phone is AWOL or dead. IMO, after the coupon, it's worth the price as long as you know what you're getting.
text_fidelity_b: 64G Mp3 Player with Bluetooth, Mp4/Story Player, Music Player, Supports FM Radio of High Volume Built-in Speaker, 4-Inch LCD Full Touch Screen, E-Book, Micro SD Card Slot Ups to 512GB (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Creative Aurvana 2 In-Ear Headphones (Discontinued by Manufacturer) Overall I'm very pleased with these ear buds. Lots of pros:

- very comfortable to wear. I always have ear buds in when working out, and these stayed put through all my cardio work with zero ear soreness.

- sound quality is great. I was listening to Friday Night in San Francisco (John Mclaughlin, Al Dimeola and Pco De Lucia) and was amazed at how much of the mid-range sound I was missing using my old ear buds (JBLs). The bass is not boomy, but more than adequate. I found I was able to get better bass sound by changing the rubber tips to a larger size that better fit my ear.

- lots of nice touches such as a carrying case that is well designed to protect the ear buds, a selection of rubber ear tips, and even a cleaning tool. It also comes with an airplane jack adapter, but I won't get much use out of that.

- outstanding sound isolation. No ambient sound gets in at all. In fact, I had to take one of them out when I was doing road work since I was concerned about not being able to hear cars approaching.

My quibbles are minor and mainly relate to the sturdiness of the cabling. It seems pretty thin and may not stand up to the rigors I often put my ear buds through. Too early to tell if this will be a problem, so I didn't subtract any stars because of it. I'll update the review should the build quality prove to be too wimpy.

Highly recommend that this be on your short list if you're looking for comfortable buds that sound great, and are very effective in blocking outside noise.

text_fidelity_a:
Dell Inspiron 14 Plus 7420 Laptop - 14 inch, 2.2K 16:10, Intel Core i7-12700H, 16GB DDR5 RAM, 1TB SSD, Intel Iris Xe, 2 Yr Onsite + AntiVirus, Migrate, Windows 11 Pro+Office 365 - Atlantic Green This laptop computer is pretty much as advertised, and I am glad to have it. The screen is sharp and readable in 2240 x 1400 pixels mode. This model does NOT have a touch screen, so if that's important to you, you need to look at other laptops that sport that feature. The system so far is quick to respond to requests and has sufficient RAM and storage space.

One nice feature missing from all the other laptops I’ve owned or used is an automatic power up whenever the computer case is opened. There is also a power button in case you need it.

Beside Windows 11 Pro, this machine comes with significant value added: a year subscription to Microsoft Office 365 (normally $69.99/year) and also a two-year subscription to McAfee LiveSafe security suite (normally $129.99/year).

Most people who use laptops probably don’t mind that this machine, like most laptops now, does not have an ethernet port. However, WiFi seems to be performing well in its absence. I may not be the typical user, but I prefer the option to connect by ethernet.

I work almost exclusively at a desk with the power supply connected, so I have not tested the battery life of this Dell. My only real complaint is that, owing to the 14” display size, the keyboard is correspondingly smaller than I like. If I were to do much typing, I’d probably plug in an external keyboard. If your hands are smaller than mine are, this won't be much of an issue for you.

As has been mentioned in other reviews, this is not a gamer’s dream machine. It’s for normal office and business use. Its compact size makes it good for the road.
text_fidelity_b: Dell Inspiron 14 Plus 7420 Laptop - 14 inch, 2.2K 16:10, Intel Core i7-12700H, 16GB DDR5 RAM, 1TB SSD, Intel Iris Xe, 2 Yr Onsite + AntiVirus, Migrate, Windows 11 Pro+Office 365 - Atlantic Green

text_fidelity_a: Techko S184S Ultra Slim Door Guard Alarm I used these while my husband was training out of state for a length of time. Both of the ones I used worked great the first night, but one went off by itself the second evening. Luckily, it was early enough to where it was still light out, and I was standing in the next room facing that direction when it went off. Otherwise, it would have scared the %$%@ out of me, thinking someone was near the door or trying to break in. I could see there was no one there, nor had there been when it first went off. The evening was still, there was no wind nor vibration, so I don't know what made it go off.  It does make a loud alarm sound, and it doesn't stop until you turn it off, so I'll give it that! It may have just been a fluke, but I didn't feel comfortable using it again. If I would have been in bed or asleep and it went off, I would have totally freaked!  I would suggest going ahead and trying these, but don't rely on them being perfect and be prepared just in case they go off by themselves.  I went ahead and went with a security system company, just to put my mind at ease.  It you can't do that at this time, I would give these a try.

**A number of free channels available through Roku. You can add a lot of content. Since I'm an old movie buff, I added Pub a Hub (public domain movies) and Crackle (pretty bad recent movies but some good classics, like Easy Rider).
**Picture is big. I have a friend who has a projector that's five times as big as the Roku, and yet the projected image is the same size. That's impressive.

CONS:
**How much radiation does this device emit? In the fine print, the instruction booklet reads: "This equipment complies with FCC radiation exposure limits set forth for an uncontrolled environment. This equipment should be installed and operated with minimum distance 20CM between the RADIATOR AND YOUR BODY."
Hmm. I don't know about you, but it's hard not to sit pretty close to the projector. I used it in the bedroom and watched a movie on the ceiling. Of course I had to be close to it in order to put it at the right angle. How much radiation is the device emitting?

**Roku asks for your credit card information before you can use the device. When you set up an account, even if you don't want anything other than the free channels, they force you to put your credit card on file. The other privacy issue I object to is the way Roku allows you to connect to Facebook. In order for Roku to work, you were pretty much forced to allow Roku to access your information on Facebook at any time (even when you're logged out!) Not happy about this.

**In order to add some channels to the Roku network, you have to establish separate accounts. That means establishing one for Netflix, one for Amazon, etc, if you don't already have one. This means I'm sharing my account information with a number of companies I may or may not want to do business with. No doubt all this information will be shared among the video providers. That means a lot of spam will be coming my way in my email.

**Roku is geared toward convincing you to subscribe to as many streaming (pay on demand) services as possible. I'm not sure I would pay $300 for it, as it is very much a device aimed to getting you to subscribe to streaming channels. You can use it other ways, but Roku feels like a product sponsored by many vendors, as opposed to a stand-alone projector.

My conclusion? I recommend it with some reservations as noted above.

The [[ASIN:B016F4AGLC other player]] handles like the [[ASIN:B0173CW2CQ first one]] I reviewed for G.G. Martinsen, but I will have to wait until I get back home to do anything other than test the recorder and FM radio on this 16GB player because I have no cable to copy music onto the player with!

Anyway, unlike the other two players, the controls on this one make sense and handle more like what I'm used to. The instructions that come with this (that I also left at home!) were well-written in English, unlike so many products coming out of China these days. But I haven't needed the instructions to figure out how to use this player or change the settings. The first thing I did was set the Power Off and Sleep settings to 0 so the player won't shut off unless I flip the manual switch to turn it off. I have been listening to this player while I've been writing reviews, and I have had absolutely no cutouts with the FM radio even though I'm in a condo sandwiched on all sides by other units and this place is bad with reception of cable TV and other radios. I like that the station stays selected even when you power the player off and on again.

The control dial is easy to see, with a top Menu button, left and right arrows, and a pause/play button on the bottom (something the other players did not have). The round button in the middle has a good tactile feel, and even in the dark it's fairly easy to feel where to press for the different functions. I'll have to re-read the instructions to understand fully when to use the center button and how.

The little piece you can thread a lanyard into is plastic, but I don't think it will break easily unless you put a lot of stress on it. The player comes with a pair of original Apple-style earphones, which are great for walking outside where you need to be able to hear sounds around you while listening to music. The headphones are not the best in the world, but they are a nice additional feature and good to have in situations where you wouldn't want pricier headphones to get ruined (the gym, outside should it start raining). Of course, your listening experience will only be as good as the wired headphones you plug into this player. It really is a whole lot of bang for the buck and an attractive little player. I have the turquoise color, and it's really nice.

I put links to the other two players I have reviewed so you can compare them. What I like about this one is it doesn't have that gimmicky bubble-gum type selection screen but, rather, just has a list of the different features and functions. The list is easy to read and looks more businesslike and professional than the more cartoonish screens of the other two players.

TP-Link Deco Mesh WiFi System(Deco M5) –Up to 5,500 sq. ft. Whole Home Coverage and 100+ Devices,WiFi Router/Extender Replacement, Anitivirus, 3-pack This review is for the TP-LInk Mesh WiFi M5 system.
—————
Amended April 28, 2020
Now that I’ve been using this for a couple weeks, I am returning to add these units HAVE NOT cured the dead spots that needed more signal strength. Yes, the WiFi signal is present in those areas of my home. However, the signal strength has not improved over what my centrally located router produced on its own. Essentially for my roughly $125, I got a couple stylish WiFi access points. What I DID NOT GET is the improved coverage promoted in the description.
—————
This IS NOT a plug it in and it works system. You need to know at minimum:
—Your current router’s IP address, the user ID for it, and the password. If you haven’t changed them from the default, you have no business installing a network anything, because you put EVERYTHING on your system at high risk for hacking. Why? The problem is that the default user ID and password are the SAME FOR ALL routers of the same brand (every brand router has a published default user id and password).
—You need to know which of several comm protocols your ISP uses.
—You need to know that IF YOU SWAP OUT YOUR ROUTER for one of the units, the others WILL NOT WORK to extend your WiFi network. For that you need to set these up as extenders, with the first being connected to your existing router.
—To set up a network of WiFi extenders, you need to know how to turn your existing router’s WiFi transmission off. Only then can you use these as extenders, satellites, or whatever you know them as.
—You are highly likely to have to update the firmware on each M5 device.
—You should set aside about two to three hours to set up a network of multiple devices.
—If you set these up as extenders, some of the default security features are switched off. You need to be sure these security features are enabled on your router instead.

I found this an unacceptably under-documented product that forces you to comb through the internet for proper setup tips. I loathe their little booklet that is “documentation” since it is a collection of single pages in multiple languages that direct you to the App Store or Google Play for the app that manages setup. That app is underpowered, has little relevant or helpful information.

I’ve been working with and installing systems from early (1990s) mainframes, Apple IIs, Macs, PCs of all flavors, and networks right up to now. Were it not for that experience, I might never have gotten this to work. Once installed, it works fine.

Recommendation: If your current router is older, you’re probably more likely to get better WiFi coverage by purchasing a newer, more current router. Try that first, and if you don't get the coverage you need, add a couple or three of these.
text_fidelity_b: TP-Link Deco Mesh WiFi System(Deco M5) –Up to 5,500 sq. ft. Whole Home Coverage and 100+ Devices,WiFi Router/Extender Replacement, Anitivirus, 3-pack

Logitech Wireless Desktop MK 300 I love my laptop; it's freed me to work in any room in the house and for that alone I'd nominate it for the greatest invention of the century. ButI don't much like the keyboard and I flat-out hate the touch pad, so I've been wanting a free-standing mouse for a while now. Along came the Logitech desktop bundle and suddenly I've got the sort of flexibility I'd been craving. They aren't kidding when they say it's ready to work right out of the box. I could do all the most basic functions without ever programming a thing. Once I installed the software, I got a lot more control. I was able to program the mouse buttons to give me single, double and right click functions as well as scrolling, the most common functions for my work. The keyboard functions include an easy application switcher, a button which boots up the default email program, and one which I've programmed to open my browser. Another key opens the control panel, and a fifth I've programmed to bring up my documents window -- a huge time-saver for a writer. There's also a key to bring up the calculator. Function keys are similarly programmable, and with the amount of choice I have I could automate all of my most common tasks and still have keys left over. There are also control keys for audio functions, and all the standard keys including a keypad which was sorely missed in my laptop. There's even a key to check battery status on both mouse and keyboard.

One of the things I liked most about the keyboard is that it can apparently be secured against keystroke monitors. Not that I have a lot of concern about that particular issue with my set-up, but people who are working in unsecured office space might well appreciate that feature.

The keys have a good, solid feel to them, and are surprisingly quiet for a stand-alone keyboard. The mouse works beautifully on a bare desk, and has a good hand feel.

If Logitech quality holds true for this duo, I look forward to many years of heavy use for both. At it's current price point, I'd call this set a bargain, and one well worth checking out.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Wireless Desktop MK 300

At first I was torn between the more expensive Oasis and this Paperwhite, and I was also confused as to why there are so many Paperwhite versions available. I figured I’d compare the newest of both to make my final decision and although the Oasis has some light features I like, I chose this Paperwhite because the side bar (where you hold it and flip pages?) on the Oasis is just ugly to me. I don’t like that it’s only on one side making the whole thing off center. I primarily wanted a Kindle so I could get off of my phone more often to just read and I also needed something that provided a more natural experience for my eyes. My favorite feature of the Kindle is that I can put it on dark mode with the black background and white text. I even keep my iPhone at the lowest light setting with dark mode too to spare my eyes the brightness 24/7.

This Kindle is exactly what I’ve been looking for. It’s lightweight, slim, very easy to hold, and turning pages is a breeze. No clicking buttons, just a tap on the screen. I paired it with the leather amazon case in plum to match and it’s perfect. Sleek and beautiful. The light options are perfect for day and night reading, I can even see it perfectly with zero eye strain in a pitch black room. The screen looks remarkably like a real print book and it’s just so simple to use. I was initially concerned about the ads being too intrusive, but it turns out that they’re only on the lock screen and they just advertise books to read. I don’t mind them at all. My Kindle is only a week old so I can’t speak to much else yet, but I’ve been using it daily all week and the battery is at 97% right now without any recharge so that gives me hope for it lasting going forward. I’m very happy with so far and have found that because it doesn’t do anything like a tablet or phone would do, I’m reading more without such distractions. Leaving my phone down more too. Love it.

SABRENT 13 Port High Speed USB 2.0 Hub with Power Adapter and 2 Control Switches (HB-U14P) This is the largest (in terms of capacity) hubs I’ve every come across. It provides 13 USB ports, but does so in a relatively compact way. 12 of the 13 ports are arranged in a row, so while the hub is long (about 8.75 inches) its only about 1.25 inches wide. Port #13 is located on the end of the strip. All ports are USB 2.0.

It has two switches to control power to the ports. Switch #1 controls ports 1 to 7; switch #2 controls the rest. The power switches are small, but are rocker style with a good feel and a positive click action. The active ports light up with a somewhat bright blue glow.

The cable to attach to your PC is fixed and rather short (8 inches). Although it’s a good, stout cable, I would have preferred that it had an input port so a longer cable could be used. As such, this is not something that would work on top of a desk that had a PC on the floor unless an extension was used (an extension is NOT included).

It does include a power supply, which is a mandatory feature for a strip with this many ports. The DC input port is next to the USB input cable.

Good build quality and a relatively compact footprint given the number of ports, but the lack of a detachable input cable drops my rating by a star.
[Sample provided for review]

ASUS VS197D-P 18.5" WXGA 1366x768 VGA Back-lit LED Monitor, Black I'm very pleased with this monitor. I needed to replace my second screen and didn't want to spend a lot, but needed a monitor with 1920x1200 resolution. This seemed like a decent bet. It has exceeded my expectations with regard to performance. The clarity is excellent -- it rivals my primary screen which cost three times as much!

The monitor is very lightweight. It comes with both DVI and VGA cables, which was unexpected. I like that there's no power transformer or wall wart. It has just a regular power cord. Set up is simple (just attached the base and no tools are needed).

Of course, at this price point some features are not present. For example, while the screen can be tilted back and forth a bit, it does not have any up/down adjustment, nor can it be swiveled into portrait mode. There's no USB connectors and no speakers. But for me, none of those were deal breakers. I wanted a good quality monitor that was affordable, and this hit the mark 100%. Plus, it does not scrimp on connections. There's DVI, VGA and HDMI. I'm using DVI at present since the PC I'm using it with is a few years old. But, my next PC will probably have a HDMI connection, making this monitor future-proof (well, as future-proof as any tech product can be).

If you're looking for a basic monitor that does not scrimp on image quality, this should definitely be on your short list. Also, check Amazon Warehouse for used ones. I got mine there (it was probably a customer's return). It looks brand new, and only ran me $127.

They work great at first, then eventually quit scrolling or, worse, get stuck in scroll mode and drive the cursor to the bottom of the page for no reason. Two have failed on me. The first was purchased in 2011 for $36, the second in 2014 for $30. Both failed to scroll reliably and made using them impossible. Other, cheaper, wireless mice work better, or at least longer.

This mouse has nice features like left/right scrolling by tilting the scroll wheel and they work on many different surfaces, but those features fall by the wayside if the thing doesn't work at all after some time.

I've tried blowing it out with compressed air to clear debris, but it didn't fix it. Haven't come to taking it apart and cleaning it, as some proffer, because it's simply not worth the time.

For how much these mice cost -- $66 for the two -- they should be bulletproof. Better to buy cheaper wireless mice and throw them away when the fail.

I'm trying the $11 [[ASIN:B074DV98R7 VicTsing 2.4G Wireless Mouse Wireless Optical Laptop Mouse with USB Nano Receiver, 6 Buttons,5 Adjustable DPI Levels,15 Months Battery Life]] next. I could have purchased six of them for what I've put into Logitech MX Anywhere mice, both of which become landfill fodder.

Logitech has lost my Anywhere MX mouse business.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Wireless Anywhere Mouse MX for PC and Mac, black

Lifeproof FRĒ SERIES iPhone 6/6s Waterproof Case (4.7" Version) - Retail Packaging - SUNSET (PIPELINE/WINDSURF/LONGBOARD) I got my mother the Lifeproof FRE case for her iPhone 6. For the last year, she’s been using a cheap case I bought on Amazon, the Diztronic Voyeur Case. I didn’t feel it was protective enough, so I hoped the Lifeproof FRE would work for her.

Unfortunately, she didn’t like the case at all, and wanted it off her phone minutes after I put it on. I made her use it for a few weeks, and while she didn’t experience any sound problems, there were several quality of life things that sealed the dislike for the Lifeproof FRE case.

PRO:
—The built-in screen protector is pretty good. I liked that I didn’t have to install it myself, as it’s part of the case.

CONS:
—Within minutes of putting the Lifeproof FRE case on her phone, I dropped it. The back of the case is slick, some kind of hard plastic instead of the grippier TPU case. The Lifeproof case just didn’t feel nice to hold in my hand, and with the slicker plastic, I worried that my mom would drop her phone as well.

—The little “door” that protects the charger port was super hard for her to open. Every time my mom wanted to charge her phone, I had to come do it for her, since she couldn’t get the door open. I understand needing a tight seal for the waterproof protection, but there has to be an easier way to access the charger port.

—The small oval cut out for charging cords was too small for my non Apple Lightning cables. I have two that are Apple certified, AmazonBasics and Zerolemon, and neither fit.

—My mom found it impossible to manipulate any of the buttons. I assume the buttons will loosen up over months, but boy, they are super hard to press when the case is new.

My mom’s not quite the intended audience for the case, but as she plans to keep her iPhone for a few years, we want it to stay in nice shape. And you never know when you’re going to drop your phone into a snowbank or puddle, so having a waterproof case adds peace of mind. But I’ll have to keep looking for her, because the Lifeproof FRE had a couple of little problems that added up to big annoyances.
text_fidelity_b: Lifeproof FRĒ SERIES iPhone 6/6s Waterproof Case (4.7" Version) - Retail Packaging - SUNSET (PIPELINE/WINDSURF/LONGBOARD)

text_fidelity_a:
Acer Aspire 3 A314-23P-R3QA Slim Laptop | 14.0" Full HD IPS Display | AMD Ryzen 5 7520U Quad-Core Processor | AMD Radeon Graphics | 8GB LPDDR5 | 512GB NVMe SSD | Wi-Fi 6 | Windows 11 Home,Silver Pros

1. Very lightweight. It weighs only 4 pounds.
2. Excellent display. It has a full HD screen resolution of 1920x1080. In particular, high resolution digital photos look great on it.
3. Screen size is excellent. It measures a generous 15.6 inches
4. Hard drive is solid state. This makes booting the laptop extremely fast. It is up and running in a mere 30-45 seconds. My previous laptop, which had a mechanical drive, took as much as 10 minutes before it was fully ready to go.
5. Battery charge is good. It lasts up to 7.5 hours.
6. Attractive, modern design. The laptop is slim and sleek, with a lovely, silver color. I especially like the visibility of the backlit keyboard.
7. Excellent price. It offers good value for the cost.

Cons

1. Processing speed is only adequate. Though the speed is probably sufficient for the average user, it could be an issue if you are doing things that require a lot of horsepower, such as editing videos or creating music in digital-audio workstation software.
2. The 4GB of RAM is minimal. This amount of RAM is the very least that any user requires these days. However, it is upgradeable.
3. The hard drive is only 128GB in size. This is a surprisingly small amount for a modern computer. However, it is probably not a problem for the average user.
4. Windows Home "S Mode" may be an issue. It is automatically enabled on the laptop as a security protection for unwary, non-techie users, who might accidentally stray into dangerous territory online that could compromise the laptop. But for the more technically advanced and self-protectively-savvy user, this feature can be very annoying. Fortunately, those same techies can easily figure out how to disable it, which allows the laptop to run the regular Windows Home version.
text_fidelity_b: Acer Aspire 3 A314-23P-R3QA Slim Laptop | 14.0" Full HD IPS Display | AMD Ryzen 5 7520U Quad-Core Processor | AMD Radeon Graphics | 8GB LPDDR5 | 512GB NVMe SSD | Wi-Fi 6 | Windows 11 Home,Silver

text_fidelity_a:
Kikkerland UL03-A Universal Travel Adapter, Black I ended up returning these. I'm going to France and the UK, which have different plug styles. I thought this would be a pretty cool way to get an adapter for each country in one neat little gadget. Well, it looks like it would work fine, but it's twice as big as a standard simple one-piece adapter. So, for size and weight, it works out the same as having a simple adapter for France and a simple adapter for the UK. And it's more than twice the price of two simple adapters, so for price it's worse. Independent of price, it doesn't make sense to me to have something complicated when there aren't any advantages over the simple solution. I'm concerned that the complexity just adds more ways for something to go wrong, and the last thing you want to do on a trip is add more ways for something to go wrong.

So, I don't think this product makes any sense if you just need on or two plug styles. However, you would start seeing a benefit if you need three or more different plug styles on your trip.
text_fidelity_b: Kikkerland UL03-A Universal Travel Adapter, Black

text_fidelity_a:
Razer Opus Active Noise Cancelling ANC Wireless Headphones: THX Audio Tuning - 25 Hr Battery - Bluetooth 4.2 & 3.5mm Jack Compatible - Auto Play/Auto Pause - Carrying Case Included - Midnight Blue At first glance, the Razer Opus ANC Wireless Headphones don’t look like a Razer product. Where’s the green? Where’s the RGB? Even the branding is subdued.

These headphones are a grown-up Razer product, probably meant to be headphones you can take anywhere and not stick out as a gamer.

The Midnight Blue color is a nice change from black. I have a few pairs of wireless headphones and every single pair is black, so I appreciate having a little variety. Midnight Blue is a very deep blue -- so deep it’s almost black.

I’ve been trying the Opus headphones out for a few weeks and they have become the headphones I use every day. Before, I was using the Sony XB900N.

My favorite thing about the Opus headphones is how comfortable they are. The headband and ear cups have cushy padding. The headphones don’t squeeze my head too tight and don’t weigh a lot. I can wear these for 5+ hours at a time and not get a headache.

Sound quality is decent. I mostly use the Opus for listening to music and TV/movies. Compared to Razer’s gaming headsets, this isn’t one I’d pick for serious gaming. There is a tiny bit of lag and the low, deep sounds aren’t as punchy as with say, a Razer Kraken headset.

Razer’s claim of up to 25 hours of battery life seems pretty accurate. I didn’t keep a log every time I used the headphones, but I was able to use them for 4-5 hours a day for a good week before needing to charge. Unfortunately there is no battery indicator on the headphones to know when the battery is running low.

I don’t love the Razer Opus app needed to tweak a few of the settings. I have an older Android phone running Nougat, the app is incompatible with my phone. So I had to borrow my mom’s iPhone to install the app. By default, the headphones shut off after 5 minutes and I could only change this setting in the app. The app also allows you to switch between a few audio presets (but you can’t create your own) and check battery life.

If I take the headphones off my head, they automatically pause whatever I’m watching or listening to. I like this; my mom often talks to me when I’m wearing headphones, so it’s a lot quicker to just take them off and now I don’t have to manually pause. This is a setting that can be changed in the app.

The Active Noise Cancelling is what I expect for a pair of headphones in this price range. It’s decent. Not great, not horrible, but good enough to mute most background noise. But I don’t like that there’s not a light or indicator on the headphones to tell when I have ANC turned on.

The Opus doesn’t support Bluetooth multipoint.

The headphones charge via USB-C. The included case stores the headphones, charging cable, USB-C to USB A adapter, 3.5 mm audio cable, and airline adapter. The case actually has an outline on the bottom to tell you how to fit the headphones inside.
text_fidelity_b: Razer Opus Active Noise Cancelling ANC Wireless Headphones: THX Audio Tuning - 25 Hr Battery - Bluetooth 4.2 & 3.5mm Jack Compatible - Auto Play/Auto Pause - Carrying Case Included - Midnight Blue

text_fidelity_a:
seenda Ergonomic Mouse, Wireless Vertical Mouse - Rechargeable Optical Mice for Multi-Purpose (Bluetooth 5.0 + Bluetooth 3.0 + USB Connection) Compatible Apple Mac and Windows Computers - Black This being the first time I have used an ergonomic mouse I had certain expectations regarding how it would solve the problem I usually have with mice. While it removes the pressure points from the center of the wrist the tilt move that point to the bone on the side of your wrist. This is easily cured by a cushioned mouse pad. So why then use it if you still need a soft spot for your wrist? Ease of use! The mouse has a variable sensitivity rate that is nice and high for us power users (move the mouse a fraction and you can span the entire screen), or dial back the sensitivity for doing very fine and slow cursor movements. The two buttons on the side are excellent as the back and forward buttons. I have become an active user of the back button. Saves having to move the mouse to the screen icon to go back.
The Bluetooth connection works about 90% of the time. When you walk away for a bit, or don't move the mouse for a while it goes to sleep. Which requires you to hit a button to make it wake back up. On my Linux environment that translates to a few seconds of time wasted on movements and button play to get Linux to realize the mouse is in play. Using the USB adapter for 2.5Gz communications, there is no waiting for anything to wake up. It simply works. Downside: it eats another port on your computer. If you have limited ports but also have Bluetooth, your best bet is to keep it on Bluetooth.
Overall I have enjoyed its speed and button options. Work very well for what I do. Takes a little getting used to but you'll be a pro in a short amount of time.
text_fidelity_b: seenda Ergonomic Mouse, Wireless Vertical Mouse - Rechargeable Optical Mice for Multi-Purpose (Bluetooth 5.0 + Bluetooth 3.0 + USB Connection) Compatible Apple Mac and Windows Computers - Black

text_fidelity_a:
iHome IHM28W2 Color Changing Alarm Clock FM Radio with USB Charging The home is a decent little alarm clock/speaker, though not always the finest in terms of design.

What does it do?
Acts as an alarm. Some people I noted were annoyed that you had to cycle through the minutes to set the time and alarm and while an hour button is easier, if you hold down the button it really zips through pretty quickly. In other words, you really don't have to plod through minute by minute. To give a sense of that, it took me 10 seconds to speed from 6:00 am to 10:00 am. So really, this isn't much of an issue in my mind. It has two alarms, which is a nice touch. The alarm can go to either the radio or to your input device, though that is a bit iffy depending on your device. It worked with my ipod touch but you're going to want to make sure your device works as it should. One problem is that it is not very easy to see in the dark.

Acts as a radio: the reception was quite good; I had no trouble with local stations. All tuned in well.

Acts as a speaker: the sound is decent for what it is. It certainly isn't going to replace your stereo or even a set of decent bluetooth speakers, but that isn't really its goal and for what it's meant to do, and what its probably target audience is (children, tweens, young teen) I'm sure it's fine.

Work with audio devices--this is a bit mixed. I've had variability with a range of Apple products. They all work in terms of producing sound, but the volume varied amongst them at times so that even with the volume all the way up on both devices it was surprisingly low. Not inaudible or anything, but not loud enough for good entertainment (probably OK for an alarm). You also just basically sit your device atop between two plastic "walls"--there's no cradle or anything and so there isn't much difference between that and just lying it flat next to or atop it. It charged my devices, but it's not a charging cradle, which would have been nicer. Instead there is a USB charge slot on the bottom of the device and you use your own charging cable. The same is true for the audio--you use a cable jack into your device (this one is provided) to link the two. It's an adequate design, if not an elegant one.

Glow/change colors: Well, it does do this. My response? Meh. But then, again, I'm really not I'm assuming the target audience. It doesn't do a anything for me, but kids and tweens might find it interesting. At the least, it isn't obnoxious (not too bright, not too fast-changing, etc.)

it's plastic, but it feels pretty hefty and the build seems decent if a little cheap. I certainly didn't have the sense that it would be fragile or break down soon or anything.

in the end, I'd say it's a decent little device for a tween sort. Not sure it's worth 50 dollars, but it's not exorbitant, just maybe a little pricey. If you're just looking for a speaker, I'd say there are bluetooth ones out there that provide better sound for the price. But if you want a speaker/alarm/radio/something to look at now and then, it's a decent purchase.
text_fidelity_b: iHome IHM28W2 Color Changing Alarm Clock FM Radio with USB Charging

text_fidelity_a:
Fujifilm FinePix T300 14 MP Digital Camera with Fujinon 10x Wide Angle Optical Zoom Lens (Black) For the non-professional photographer looking to get high-quality images in a variety of settings, this camera works great. I did a little experiment to see how it performed by taking it with me to Europe along with a much more expensive semi-professional Nikon (D3100). Here are the results:

Advantages:
-With our limited time, my camera was able to take a variety of shots (panoramic, zoom, close-up) quickly and easily while the Nikon could only take limited kinds because of the need to bring several lenses and because of the complexity (sometimes) of setting up a given shot
-Because it was small, I didn't have to lug around a big camera bag, which also had the potential of getting a little too much unwanted attention
-One feature I really enjoyed was the two simultaneous flash/no flash shot which gives you the same picture with and without flash, letting you choose later which you prefer
-Didn't need more than one lens
-With city shots of architecture, my camera fared better with its versatility

Disadvantages:
-In the mountains, the Nikon did better, capturing color and clarity/detail. In my shots, the trees looked less defined from high up. Also, his zoom lens was able to capture much more detail than my camera.
-Nature shots and portraits have slightly duller colors, missing something the other camera was able to capture
-There was slightly more blur in shots with movement with this camera

Conclusion:
For the price, this camera performed much better than I expected and was not as much of a hassle as our semi-professional camera, so for most people, this is not only going to be a better value, but less frustrating and cumbersome. For the professional, this is obviously not the best choice, but this isn't being marketed as a professional camera. This is a great family and vacation camera that everyone can use, and that still yields quality images with plenty of artistic integrity.
Great little camera, and fun to use!

**see pics for some examples of how this camera performed**
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm FinePix T300 14 MP Digital Camera with Fujinon 10x Wide Angle Optical Zoom Lens (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Apple Lightning to USB Cable (2 m) IMO Apple cords still seem to work the best for Apple products. I really like the added length of this 2M cord (6.6'). I have tried many other cords that seem to work for a while, but always seem to fail sooner than Apple cords. My only complaints w/Apple cords are they are more expensive than after market cords and seem to be more fragile, particularly near the Lightening connector end. But, they do work until they literally break. I've had cords where the sheath is torn away and the inside wires are all hanging out, but as long they are connected the cable will charge. To remedy this problem, I have put CableCollars on all of my Apple cords to help reinforce the ends. This is something I wish Apple would do at the manufacturer. For Apple products, I definitely recommend Apple cords.

Update 5Aug2020: My 2m Apple iPhone charging cord is still holding up and working fine. I also just purchased a .5m cord to use on my motorcycle where I only needed a short cord to keep my iPhone charged. I like that it is an Apple cord and came in an Apple box.
text_fidelity_b: Apple Lightning to USB Cable (2 m)

text_fidelity_a:
occiam Bluetooth Headphones 4-Mics Call Waterproof Wireless Earbuds Over Ear Earphones with 2200mAh Wireless Charging Case for Sports Running Workout Gaming Blue This is definitely one of the better pairs of earbuds I've purchased. The pairing, which can sometimes be frustrating, was incredibly simple with these. They came already charged, and were ready for use.

I tested their range throughout my house, and they did great. I didn't notice any problems leaving my phone upstairs, and going in every room downstairs. So the range of coverage is really good.

The charging case displays the percentage of charge remaining. This is a great feature, and keeps me from having to guess if I have enough charge for use if I forget to charge them. The charging case can also be used to charge other devices, but I haven't tried this out yet.

They fit comfortably in my ear, and are more secure than my pop in earbuds. My pop ins will sometimes pop out if I'm too active. I did have to change the rubber earpieces to get a better fit, but there are several included so it was easy to get a good fit.

I think these are a very good value for the money. They perform as well as many more expensive earbuds, but won't break the bank.

text_fidelity_a:
Sabrent 4 Port Mini Portable USB 3.0 Hub [2-ft Cable] (HB-MNBW) In appearance, this is a streamlined, attractive-looking USB hub. It looks good on my desk.

I use this device as a USB hub for my desktop PC to connect three external hard drives, to backup my iPhone to my computer, to load my MP3 device, and to charge a small desk fan. I have also used it attached to my laptop for similar purposes. For all these situations, it works very well.

I have not attempted to use this USB hub as a power strip, plugged to a wall outlet using an adapter, in order to charge devices. I have other faster and more efficient wall-outlet-charging products specifically made for that purpose. I understand from the manufacturer that this device is not made for that purpose and will act as a very slow, "trickle" charger because "the devices connected to this hub must not exceed a power draw of 5 volts 900 mA for USB 3.0."

All in all, this is an excellent, basic, USB hub.
text_fidelity_b: Sabrent 4 Port Mini Portable USB 3.0 Hub [2-ft Cable] (HB-MNBW)
